The story is set in the early 1900s, a time when the Inuit were in the midst of a major cultural change. More than anything else, the people of Egulac wanted trade goods, and they got most of their trade goods from the white men in the nearby prospectors' camps. Because of their desire for trade goods, the Inuit were often forced to barter with the white men on the prospectors' terms. In the story, the two men are traveling between camps because they are looking for a new source of trade goods. They are therefore willing to travel long distances across the frozen lake in search of a new trade partner.

Analysis
This story is an example of the theme of "taming the wild", which is present in many other stories of the Canoe Boys series. In this story, the boys are camping in the wild and are visited by two men from a local Native American tribe, who are depicted as "savage" and threatening. Through the use of dialogue and action, the boys demonstrate their ability to assert dominance over the Native Americans, through actions such as cutting a pole in half and breaking a rifle in half with their bare hands. Background
The story is part of a collection of Inuit tales, retold by Haining. The purpose of the collection was to provide examples of the folklore of the Inuit people, thus providing insight into their culture and way of life.

Analysis
The tale is a good example of the type of punishment meted out in Inuit society for breaking a taboo. In this tale, the two men were punished for wasting valuable time. By getting drunk, they were not hunting and therefore not providing for themselves or their families. This type of behavior was not tolerated and so the men were left to die.

Background
The incident took place in 1871 along the banks of the Fraser River, in what is now British Columbia. The Egulac, or Syilx, people were angry because the whiskey traders had given them bad whiskey, which they said made them sick. They came to the camp of the Whitford and Dewdney treaties signing party to obtain fresh horses and weapons, but when they saw the whiskey they demanded the whites give them all of it. When the whites refused they became angry and threatened to attack. 
The camp was completely surrounded by the Egulac, who were armed with a number of rifles and several hundred swords and sabres. The whites were unarmed. After a long negotiation the Egulac agreed to depart, but as they left they cut the tents and stole the horses. When the whites attempted to recover their horses they were attacked and several were wounded. 
This incident was one of a series of incidents which led to the Fraser River Indian War.

The answer is: a native tribe of northeastern Saskatchewan, Canada, came to a trading post to trade furs. One of the men, named Pakan, was the chief of the band. While they were there, a group of bandits came to the trading post and attacked the two men, stripping them of their furs and other possessions. When they did return, they were surprised to find the two men had not moved from where they had left them. Upon inquiring as to the men's health, the men said that they were fine. The traders then left the men again, and did not return for several more days. This time, when they returned, they were shocked to find that the men had died while they were gone.

Analysis
This story is an example of the stereotype of the incompetent native. The Egulac men were incompetent in that they could not protect themselves from bandits, and they were unable to move from one place to another without assistance. The story implies that had the Egulac men been competent, they would have been able to protect themselves from the bandits and thus would not have died.

The story also contains an element of the magical thinking common to many native cultures. The men were able to communicate with the traders even when they were supposedly dead, and their bodies were apparently unable to decay for an extended period of time.

Source
